subproblem.title: Lemma S: closed sets invariant under small affine maps along a subspace
subproblem.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, let S ⊆ ℝ^P be closed and let L ⊆ ℝ^P be a linear subspace such that {x : y + λx ∈ S} = S whenever y ∈ L, 0 < λ < 1 and |y| ≤ 1 − λ. Then (i) y + λz ∈ S ⇔ z ∈ S for all y ∈ L, all λ > 0 and all z ∈ ℝ^P; and (ii) if S ≠ ∅ then L ⊆ S.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (S : Set (Euclid P)) (L : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), IsClosed S → (∀ y ∈ L, ∀ lam : ℝ, 0 < lam → lam < 1 → ‖y‖ ≤ 1 - lam → (fun x => y + lam • x) ⁻¹' S = S) → (∀ y ∈ L, ∀ lam : ℝ, 0 < lam → ∀ z, y + lam • z ∈ S ↔ z ∈ S) ∧ (S.Nonempty → (L : Set (Euclid P)) ⊆ S)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Lemma S of the parent proof (step 2), i.e. the uses of A.3(2) in Simon's proof of A.4: chapter-A.txt lines 135–136 ('hence sing ψ ⊇ T by A.3(2)') and lines 150–152 ('together with A.3(2) gives L ⊆ sing ψ'). Here they are stated for a closed set S invariant under the small affine maps x ↦ y + λx with y ∈ L.
Notation: for y ∈ ℝ^P and λ > 0 let T_{y,λ}(z) := y + λz. Let G be the set of pairs (y, λ) with y ∈ L, λ > 0 and T_{y,λ}(z) ∈ S ⇔ z ∈ S for every z ∈ ℝ^P. The hypothesis says exactly that (y, λ) ∈ G whenever y ∈ L, 0 < λ < 1 and |y| ≤ 1 − λ.
1. Composition. If (y₁, λ₁) and (y₂, λ₂) are in G, then (y₁ + λ₁y₂, λ₁λ₂) ∈ G. Indeed y₁ + λ₁y₂ ∈ L, λ₁λ₂ > 0, and T_{y₁,λ₁}∘T_{y₂,λ₂} = T_{y₁+λ₁y₂, λ₁λ₂}. Hence T_{y₁+λ₁y₂,λ₁λ₂}(z) ∈ S ⇔ T_{y₂,λ₂}(z) ∈ S ⇔ z ∈ S.
2. Inverses. If (y, λ) ∈ G then (−λ⁻¹y, λ⁻¹) ∈ G. Indeed −λ⁻¹y ∈ L, and for z ∈ ℝ^P the point w := −λ⁻¹y + λ⁻¹z satisfies T_{y,λ}(w) = z, so w ∈ S ⇔ z ∈ S.
3. Dilations. For 0 < λ < 1, (0, λ) ∈ G by hypothesis, since |0| = 0 ≤ 1 − λ. (0, 1) ∈ G trivially. For λ > 1, (0, λ⁻¹) ∈ G, and step 2 gives (0, λ) ∈ G.
4. Short translations. Let a ∈ L with |a| ≤ 1/2. Then (a, 1/2) ∈ G by hypothesis and (0, 2) ∈ G by step 3. Step 1 gives (a + (1/2)·0, (1/2)·2) = (a, 1) ∈ G.
5. All translations. Let y ∈ L and choose an integer m ≥ 1 with |y|/m ≤ 1/2. By step 4, (y/m, 1) ∈ G. If (jy/m, 1) ∈ G, step 1 applied to (jy/m, 1) and (y/m, 1) gives ((j+1)y/m, 1) ∈ G. By induction, (y, 1) ∈ G.
6. Part (i). Let y ∈ L and λ > 0. Then (y, 1) ∈ G by step 5 and (0, λ) ∈ G by step 3, so step 1 gives (y + 1·0, 1·λ) = (y, λ) ∈ G. That is, y + λz ∈ S ⇔ z ∈ S for every z.
7. Part (ii). Let z ∈ S and y ∈ L. For 0 < λ < 1, part (i) gives y + λz ∈ S. As λ ↓ 0, y + λz → y, so y lies in the closure of S, which is S. Hence L ⊆ S. ∎
proof_key_steps: the admissible pairs (y,λ) are closed under composition and inversion of the affine maps z ↦ y+λz
this generates every dilation λ>0 and every translation by a short vector of L
translations by arbitrary y ∈ L are compositions of short ones, which gives (i)
letting λ↓0 in y+λz ∈ S and using closedness gives L ⊆ S

audit.reason: The proposition exactly expresses both conclusions. Composition and inversion generate all positive dilations and subspace translations from the permitted maps. Closedness then gives L ⊆ S by letting the dilation tend to zero.

subproblem.title: Upper density of Hausdorff content (Simon Ch. 1, 3.26(2)) in cover form
subproblem.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, ℓ > 0 and let A ⊆ ℝ^P be a bounded Borel set. Then the set of x ∈ A for which the following property fails has μH[ℓ] outer measure 0: for every δ > 0 there is ρ ∈ (0, δ) such that every countable cover {C_j}_{j∈ℕ} of A ∩ B_ρ(x) satisfies ρ^ℓ ≤ 2·Σ_j (diam C_j)^ℓ, with diameters in [0, ∞] and diam ∅ = 0.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (ℓ : ℝ) (A : Set (Euclid P)), 0 < ℓ → MeasurableSet A → Bornology.IsBounded A → μH[ℓ] {x | x ∈ A ∧ ¬ ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∃ ρ : ℝ, 0 < ρ ∧ ρ < δ ∧ ∀ C : ℕ → Set (Euclid P), A ∩ ball x ρ ⊆ ⋃ j, C j → ENNReal.ofReal ρ ^ ℓ ≤ 2 * ∑' j, Metric.ediam (C j) ^ ℓ} = 0
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 3.26(2) (chapter-01.txt lines 1197–1240): Θ^{*n}(H^n_∞, A, x) ≥ 2^{−n} for H^n-a.e. x ∈ A. This is the bound Simon cites as '3.6(2) of Ch. 1' at chapter-A.txt line 72, and it is used in step 0(d) and step 5 of the parent. Here it is stated in unnormalized cover form.
The pinned library proves it as Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.simon_theorem_3_26_ii_of_totallyBounded (axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). That lemma needs Carathéodory measurability, which follows from MeasurableSet A, and its normalized outer measure has the same null sets as μH[ℓ] by simonHausdorffOuterMeasureReal_eq_scaled_hausdorffMeasure. A self-contained proof follows.
Notation: for E ⊆ ℝ^P and τ ∈ (0, ∞] let h_τ(E) := inf{Σ_j (diam C_j)^ℓ : E ⊆ ∪_{j∈ℕ} C_j, diam C_j < τ for all j}. Here diam ∅ = 0 and 0^ℓ = 0 since ℓ > 0.
Facts:
(a) h_τ is monotone and countably subadditive.
(b) h_∞ ≤ h_τ.
(c) If diam E < τ then h_τ(E) = h_∞(E): any cover {D_i} of E can be replaced by {D_i ∩ E}, whose diameters are ≤ diam E < τ and whose sum is no larger.
(d) μH[ℓ](E) = sup_{τ>0} h_τ(E). Mathlib's definition uses diam ≤ τ, which gives the same supremum, because the families with diam < τ lie between those with diam ≤ τ/2 and those with diam ≤ τ.
(e) For bounded A, h_τ(A) < ∞ for every τ > 0: cover the compact closure of A by finitely many balls of radius τ/3.
1. A point x ∈ A fails the property iff there is δ > 0 with h_∞(A ∩ B_ρ(x)) < ρ^ℓ/2 for every ρ ∈ (0, δ). (A cover with 2Σ(diam C_j)^ℓ < ρ^ℓ exists iff h_∞ < ρ^ℓ/2.) For m ≥ 1 let N_m := {x ∈ A : h_∞(A ∩ B_ρ(x)) < ρ^ℓ/2 for all ρ ∈ (0, 1/m)}. The exceptional set is ∪_m N_m, so it suffices to show μH[ℓ](N_m) = 0 for every m.
2. Fix m, put δ := 1/m, and fix τ ∈ (0, δ). By (e), h_τ(N_m) ≤ h_τ(A) < ∞. Let ε > 0. Choose a cover {C_j} of N_m with diam C_j < τ and Σ_j (diam C_j)^ℓ ≤ h_τ(N_m) + ε. Drop the C_j that do not meet N_m, and pick x_j ∈ C_j ∩ N_m. Let d_j := diam C_j ∈ [0, τ).
3. By continuity of t ↦ t^ℓ, choose ρ_j ∈ (d_j, δ) with ρ_j^ℓ ≤ d_j^ℓ + ε2^{−j−1}. Then E_j := C_j ∩ N_m ⊆ B̄_{d_j}(x_j) ∩ A ⊆ A ∩ B_{ρ_j}(x_j).
4. Since x_j ∈ N_m and 0 < ρ_j < δ, h_∞(A ∩ B_{ρ_j}(x_j)) < ρ_j^ℓ/2. As diam E_j ≤ d_j < τ, fact (c) and monotonicity give h_τ(E_j) = h_∞(E_j) ≤ h_∞(A ∩ B_{ρ_j}(x_j)) < ρ_j^ℓ/2 ≤ (d_j^ℓ + ε2^{−j−1})/2.
5. N_m = ∪_j E_j, so by (a), h_τ(N_m) ≤ Σ_j h_τ(E_j) ≤ (1/2)Σ_j d_j^ℓ + ε/2 ≤ (1/2)(h_τ(N_m) + ε) + ε/2. Since h_τ(N_m) < ∞, this gives h_τ(N_m) ≤ 2ε. As ε is arbitrary, h_τ(N_m) = 0.
6. This holds for every τ ∈ (0, δ), and h_τ increases as τ decreases. So by (d), μH[ℓ](N_m) = sup_{0<τ<δ} h_τ(N_m) = 0. By countable subadditivity, the exceptional set ∪_m N_m is μH[ℓ]-null. ∎
proof_key_steps: exceptional points satisfy h_∞(A∩B_ρ(x)) < ρ^ℓ/2 for all small ρ; group them by the scale 1/m into sets N_m
cover N_m by sets C_j of diameter < τ that meet N_m, and enlarge each to a ball B_{ρ_j}(x_j) with ρ_j^ℓ ≈ (diam C_j)^ℓ
for sets of diameter < τ, h_τ = h_∞; hence h_τ(N_m) ≤ ½(h_τ(N_m)+ε)+ε/2, which forces h_τ(N_m)=0
taking the supremum over τ gives μH[ℓ](N_m)=0

audit.reason: The Lean proposition faithfully uses extended diameters, real powers and outer-null exceptional sets. The self-contained covering argument is complete: boundedness gives finite fixed-scale content, intersection with small-diameter sets identifies the two contents, and the contraction estimate forces each exceptional set N_m to be Hausdorff-null. No finite Hausdorff-measure assumption is needed.

subproblem.title: Remark A.5: invariance under a subspace of dimension ≥ n forces a plane indicator
subproblem.statement: Let P, n, Q ∈ ℕ, let ψ : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q be locally μH[n]-integrable, and let L ⊆ ℝ^P be a linear subspace with dim L ≥ n such that ψ(y + λx) = ψ(x) for all y ∈ L, λ > 0 and x ∈ ℝ^P. Then there is an n-dimensional linear subspace L' ⊆ ℝ^P with ψ = ψ(0)·1_{L'} everywhere on ℝ^P.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P n Q : ℕ) (ψ : Euclid P → Euclid Q) (L : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), LocallyIntegrable ψ μH[(n : ℝ)] → n ≤ Module.finrank ℝ L → (∀ y ∈ L, ∀ lam : ℝ, 0 < lam → ∀ x, ψ (y + lam • x) = ψ x) → ∃ L' : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P), Module.finrank ℝ L' = n ∧ ψ = Set.indicator (L' : Set (Euclid P)) (fun _ => ψ 0)
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, Remark A.5 (chapter-A.txt lines 46–50), as expanded in step 3 of the parent proof. Write μ := μH[n] on ℝ^P.
1. Since dim L ≥ n, choose n linearly independent vectors in L and let L' be their span. Then L' is an n-dimensional linear subspace with L' ⊆ L.
2. For y ∈ L', invariance with x = 0 and λ = 1 gives ψ(y) = ψ(y + 1·0) = ψ(0). So ψ = ψ(0) on L', and it remains to show ψ(x) = 0 for every x ∉ L'.
3. Fix x ∉ L'. Then V := L' + ℝx is a linear subspace of dimension n + 1. Every v ∈ V can be written uniquely as v = y + tx with y ∈ L' and t ∈ ℝ, and τ(v) := t is a linear functional on V. Let H := {v ∈ V : τ(v) > 0} = {y + λx : y ∈ L', λ > 0}. For y ∈ L' ⊆ L and λ > 0, invariance gives ψ(y + λx) = ψ(x). Hence ψ ≡ ψ(x) on H.
4. Suppose ψ(x) ≠ 0. Local integrability at the point x gives r > 0 with ∫_{B_r(x)} |ψ| dμ < ∞.
5. τ is continuous on the finite-dimensional space V and τ(x) = 1 > 0. So H is relatively open in V and contains x, and we can choose r' ∈ (0, r] with E := V ∩ B_{r'}(x) ⊆ H. E is Borel (a closed subspace intersected with an open ball), nonempty, convex and open relative to V. Its affine span is therefore V, so its Hausdorff dimension is dim V = n + 1 (Mathlib Convex.dimH_eq_finrank_vectorSpan). Since n < n + 1 = dim_H E, μH[n](E) = ∞ (Mathlib hausdorffMeasure_of_lt_dimH).
6. E ⊆ H ∩ B_r(x) and ψ ≡ ψ(x) on E, so ∫_{B_r(x)} |ψ| dμ ≥ ∫_E |ψ| dμ = |ψ(x)|·μ(E) = ∞. This contradicts step 4, hence ψ(x) = 0.
7. By steps 2 and 6, ψ(x) = ψ(0) for x ∈ L' and ψ(x) = 0 for x ∉ L'. That is, ψ = ψ(0)·1_{L'} everywhere, with dim L' = n. If L' = ℝ^P, step 3 is vacuous. ∎
proof_key_steps: choose an n-dimensional L' ⊆ L; invariance makes ψ ≡ ψ(0) on L'
for x ∉ L', invariance makes ψ ≡ ψ(x) on the half (n+1)-plane {y+λx : y∈L', λ>0}, which is relatively open in L'+ℝx
a nonempty relatively open piece of an (n+1)-plane has dimH = n+1, so its μH[n] measure is infinite
local integrability at x forces ψ(x)=0, so ψ = ψ(0)·1_{L'}

audit.reason: The type matches the pointwise indicator conclusion. The proof constructs an n-dimensional subspace inside L and shows that any nonzero value outside it would persist on a relatively open (n+1)-dimensional piece of infinite μH[n] measure, contradicting local integrability. The zero-dimensional and full-subspace cases are covered.

subproblem.title: Lemma T: limits of singular points are singular for the weak limit
subproblem.statement: Let P, n, Q ∈ ℕ, let F be a set of functions ℝ^P → ℝ^Q and let sing map functions ℝ^P → ℝ^Q to subsets of ℝ^P. Write φ_k ⇀ φ if ∫ f·φ_k dμH[n] → ∫ f·φ dμH[n] for every continuous compactly supported f : ℝ^P → ℝ. Assume (A.3c) sing φ is closed for every φ ∈ F, and (A.3(3)) whenever φ ∈ F, φ_k ∈ F and φ_k ⇀ φ, for every ε > 0 there is k₀ with B_1(0) ∩ sing φ_k ⊆ {x : ∃ z ∈ sing φ, |x − z| < ε} for all k ≥ k₀. If ψ ∈ F, φ_k ∈ F for all k, φ_k ⇀ ψ, z_k ∈ B_1(0) ∩ sing φ_k for every k and z_k → z, then z ∈ sing ψ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P n Q : ℕ) (F : Set (Euclid P → Euclid Q)) (sing : (Euclid P → Euclid Q) → Set (Euclid P)), (∀ φ ∈ F, IsClosed (sing φ)) → (∀ φ ∈ F, ∀ φs : ℕ → Euclid P → Euclid Q, (∀ k, φs k ∈ F) → (∀ f : Euclid P → ℝ, Continuous f → HasCompactSupport f → Tendsto (fun k => ∫ x, f x • φs k x ∂μH[(n : ℝ)]) atTop (𝓝 (∫ x, f x • φ x ∂μH[(n : ℝ)]))) → ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ k₀ : ℕ, ∀ k ≥ k₀, ball (0 : Euclid P) 1 ∩ sing (φs k) ⊆ {x | ∃ z ∈ sing φ, dist x z < ε}) → ∀ ψ ∈ F, ∀ φs : ℕ → Euclid P → Euclid Q, (∀ k, φs k ∈ F) → (∀ f : Euclid P → ℝ, Continuous f → HasCompactSupport f → Tendsto (fun k => ∫ x, f x • φs k x ∂μH[(n : ℝ)]) atTop (𝓝 (∫ x, f x • ψ x ∂μH[(n : ℝ)]))) → ∀ (zs : ℕ → Euclid P) (z : Euclid P), (∀ k, zs k ∈ ball (0 : Euclid P) 1 ∩ sing (φs k)) → Tendsto zs atTop (𝓝 z) → z ∈ sing ψ
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Lemma T of the parent proof (step 1), in the general form used in parent steps 4, 8 and 9. Simon, proof of A.4, chapter-A.txt line 135 ('sing ψ ≠ ∅ (by A.3(3))') and lines 150–151 ('{ξ/2} ⊆ sing ψ by A.3(2), (3)').
1. Let ε > 0. Apply A.3(3) to ψ ∈ F, the sequence φ_k ∈ F (which converges weakly to ψ) and ε/2. This gives k₀ such that for all k ≥ k₀, B_1(0) ∩ sing φ_k ⊆ {w : ∃ v ∈ sing ψ, |w − v| < ε/2}.
2. Since z_k ∈ B_1(0) ∩ sing φ_k, step 1 gives for every k ≥ k₀ a point v_k ∈ sing ψ with |z_k − v_k| < ε/2.
3. Since z_k → z, there is k₁ with |z_k − z| < ε/2 for all k ≥ k₁. For k := max(k₀, k₁), |z − v_k| ≤ |z − z_k| + |z_k − v_k| < ε. So for every ε > 0 the ball B_ε(z) meets sing ψ, i.e. z lies in the closure of sing ψ.
4. sing ψ is closed because ψ ∈ F (A.3c), so z ∈ sing ψ. ∎
proof_key_steps: A.3(3) with ε/2 places each z_k (k large) within ε/2 of a point of sing ψ
z_k → z places z within ε of sing ψ for every ε > 0
sing ψ is closed, hence z ∈ sing ψ

audit.reason: The type matches all stated hypotheses. Upper semicontinuity with ε/2 and convergence of the singular points place the limit in the closure of sing ψ; closedness proves membership. The argument also correctly excludes an empty limiting singular set.

subproblem.title: Weak convergence survives translations and dilations with factors tending to 1
subproblem.statement: Let P, n, Q ∈ ℕ and μ := μH[n] on ℝ^P. Let g_k : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q (k ∈ ℕ) be locally μ-integrable, let g : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q be arbitrary, let y ∈ ℝ^P, and let c_k > 0 with c_k → 1. Suppose ∫ f g_k dμ → ∫ f g dμ for every continuous compactly supported f : ℝ^P → ℝ. Then for every such f, ∫ f(x) g_k(y + c_k x) dμ(x) → ∫ f(x) g(y + x) dμ(x).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P n Q : ℕ) (gs : ℕ → Euclid P → Euclid Q) (g : Euclid P → Euclid Q) (y : Euclid P) (mus : ℕ → ℝ), (∀ k, LocallyIntegrable (gs k) μH[(n : ℝ)]) → (∀ k, 0 < mus k) → Tendsto mus atTop (𝓝 1) → (∀ f : Euclid P → ℝ, Continuous f → HasCompactSupport f → Tendsto (fun k => ∫ x, f x • gs k x ∂μH[(n : ℝ)]) atTop (𝓝 (∫ x, f x • g x ∂μH[(n : ℝ)]))) → ∀ f : Euclid P → ℝ, Continuous f → HasCompactSupport f → Tendsto (fun k => ∫ x, f x • gs k (y + mus k • x) ∂μH[(n : ℝ)]) atTop (𝓝 (∫ x, f x • g (y + x) ∂μH[(n : ℝ)]))
subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: facts (b) and (c) of the parent proof (step 0) and its departure [D2]. The weak limits in Simon's chapter-A.txt lines 125–133 ('ψ_{βx,1} = lim φ_{x+λ_jβx,λ_j} = ψ') need the uniform bound proved below. Write μ := μH[n] and c_k := mus k.
1. Change of variables. Let c > 0, y ∈ ℝ^P and T(x) := y + cx. Hausdorff measure is translation invariant and satisfies μH[n](cA) = c^n μH[n](A) (Mathlib hausdorffMeasure_smul₀, map_homothety_hausdorffMeasure). So μ(T⁻¹B) = μ(c⁻¹(B − y)) = c^{−n}μ(B) for Borel B, i.e. T_#μ = c^{−n}μ. Since T is a measurable embedding, ∫ h(y + cx) dμ(x) = ∫ h d(T_#μ) = c^{−n}∫ h dμ for every h : ℝ^P → ℝ^Q. If h is not integrable, then neither is h∘T, and both sides are 0.
2. Fix f continuous with spt f ⊆ B̄_R(0), R > 0. Put f_k(w) := f((w − y)/c_k) and f_∞(w) := f(w − y). Step 1 gives ∫ f(x) g_k(y + c_k x) dμ(x) = c_k^{−n} ∫ f_k g_k dμ and ∫ f(x) g(y + x) dμ(x) = ∫ f_∞ g dμ.

4. Uniform bound (Banach–Steinhaus). Let X_K be the space of bounded continuous h : ℝ^P → ℝ with h = 0 outside K, with the sup norm. It is a closed subspace of the Banach space of bounded continuous functions, hence complete. For each k, Λ_k(h) := ∫ h g_k dμ is a linear map X_K → ℝ^Q with |Λ_k(h)| ≤ ‖h‖_∞ ∫_K |g_k| dμ < ∞, because g_k is locally integrable and K is compact. So Λ_k is a bounded operator. Every h ∈ X_K is continuous with compact support (spt h ⊆ K), so (Λ_k h)_k converges by hypothesis and is bounded. the rescaled test functions f((w−y)/c_k) converge uniformly to f(w−y), with supports in a fixed compact K
Banach–Steinhaus on the complete space of bounded continuous functions vanishing off K bounds h ↦ ∫h g_k uniformly in k

subproblem.title: Step 9: when d = 0 the singular sets are locally finite in B_1(0)
subproblem.statement: Let P, n, Q ∈ ℕ, F and sing satisfy A.1, A.2, A.3c, A.3(2) and A.3(3) as in the parent theorem (weak convergence taken with respect to μH[n]). Suppose μH[1](sing φ ∩ B_1(0)) = 0 for every φ ∈ F. Then sing φ ∩ B_σ(0) is finite for every φ ∈ F and every real σ < 1.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, proof of A.4, last paragraph, chapter-A.txt lines 142–153, i.e. step 9 of the parent proof. The hypothesis μH[1](sing φ ∩ B_1(0)) = 0 is Simon's (5) with α = 1.
1. Let φ ∈ F and σ < 1, and suppose Σ := sing φ ∩ B_σ(0) is infinite (so σ > 0). Choose pairwise distinct points p_k ∈ Σ, k ∈ ℕ.
2. Accumulation point. The p_k lie in the compact ball B̄_σ(0), so a subsequence converges to some x with |x| ≤ σ < 1, and x ∈ sing φ because sing φ is closed. Since the p_k are distinct, at most one of them equals x. Deleting it gives a sequence q_k ∈ sing φ with q_k ≠ x and q_k → x.
3. Normalization. Let a_k := 2|q_k − x|; then a_k > 0 and a_k → 0. Choose indices inductively, each larger than the previous one, with a strictly smaller value of a that does not exceed (1 − |x|)/2; this is possible because a_k → 0 and a_k > 0. Along the resulting subsequence, a_k is strictly decreasing and a_k ≤ (1 − |x|)/2. The unit vectors u_k := (q_k − x)/|q_k − x| lie in the compact unit sphere, so we can pass to a further subsequence with u_k → ξ, |ξ| = 1. Strict decrease and the bound persist along subsequences; keep the names q_k, a_k, u_k.
4. Tangent function. Apply (A.2) with y = x (|x| < 1) to the sequence a_k. This gives a strictly increasing sub and ψ ∈ F, homogeneous of degree zero, with φ_{x,λ_k} ⇀ ψ, where λ_k := a_{sub(k)}. Since 0 < λ_k ≤ (1 − |x|)/2 < 1 and |x| ≤ 1 − λ_k, (A.1) gives φ_k := φ_{x,λ_k} ∈ F, and (A.3(2)) gives sing φ_k = {z : x + λ_k z ∈ sing φ}.
5. A singular point of ψ. Let z_k := (q_{sub(k)} − x)/λ_k = u_{sub(k)}/2. Then |z_k| = 1/2, so z_k ∈ B_1(0). Also x + λ_k z_k = q_{sub(k)} ∈ sing φ, so z_k ∈ sing φ_k. As z_k → ξ/2, the sibling lemma adr_sing_mem_of_tendsto gives ξ/2 ∈ sing ψ.
6. A singular ray. By homogeneity ψ_{0,λ} = ψ for λ > 0, so (A.3(2)) gives sing ψ = {z : λz ∈ sing ψ} for 0 < λ < 1, and sing ψ is closed. The sibling lemma adr_affine_invariant_closed_set with L = {0} gives λz ∈ sing ψ ⇔ z ∈ sing ψ for all λ > 0. Hence tξ ∈ sing ψ for all t > 0.
7. Contradiction. The segment {tξ : 1/4 ≤ t ≤ 1/2} lies in sing ψ ∩ B_1(0), since |tξ| = t < 1. Its μH[1]-measure equals its length 1/4 (Mathlib hausdorffMeasure_segment). So μH[1](sing ψ ∩ B_1(0)) ≥ 1/4 > 0, contradicting the hypothesis for ψ ∈ F. Hence Σ is finite. ∎
proof_key_steps: an infinite singular set in B_σ(0) has an accumulation point x ∈ sing φ with |x| < 1, approached by distinct singular points
pass to subsequences with strictly decreasing scales λ = 2|q−x| and convergent directions ξ; A.2 gives a homogeneous tangent function ψ
the rescaled points (q−x)/λ (norm 1/2) are singular for the blow-ups, so ξ/2 ∈ sing ψ (sibling Lemma T)
Lemma S (sibling, L={0}) gives the whole ray in sing ψ; a segment of μH[1]-measure 1/4 contradicts the hypothesis

audit.reason: The contract matches the sufficient hypothesis that every unit-ball singular set is μH[1]-null. The proof obtains an interior accumulation point, admissible strictly decreasing scales and convergent directions. The declared lemmas produce a singular ray containing a segment of measure 1/4, contradicting nullity. For σ ≤ 0 the ball is empty.

subproblem.title: Lemma I: tangent functions inherit invariance plus the blow-up direction
subproblem.statement: Let P, n, Q ∈ ℕ and let F be a set of functions ℝ^P → ℝ^Q. Write φ_{y,λ}(x) := φ(y + λx), and let ⇀ denote convergence of ∫ f·(·) dμH[n] for every continuous compactly supported f : ℝ^P → ℝ. Assume (H0) two members of F agreeing μH[n]-a.e. are equal; (H1) every member of F is locally μH[n]-integrable; (A.1) φ_{y,λ} ∈ F whenever φ ∈ F, 0 < λ < 1 and |y| ≤ 1 − λ. Let φ ∈ F and let S be a linear subspace with φ(y + λx) = φ(x) for all y ∈ S, λ > 0 and x. Let x ∈ ℝ^P, and let λ_k > 0 with λ_k → 0 and φ_{x,λ_k} ∈ F for all k. Let ψ ∈ F with ψ(λz) = ψ(z) for all λ > 0 and z, and φ_{x,λ_k} ⇀ ψ. Then ψ(y + λz) = ψ(z) for all y ∈ S + ℝx, all λ > 0 and all z.

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, proof of A.4, chapter-A.txt lines 125–134: ψ_{y,1} = ψ for y ∈ S and ψ_{βx,1} = ψ for β ∈ ℝ, hence invariance under the span of S and x. This is Lemma I (step 6) of the parent proof, with its departure [D2]. The parent's hypotheses x ∈ B_1(0) and λ_k decreasing are replaced by the only consequence used, φ_{x,λ_k} ∈ F. Write μ := μH[n] and g_k(z) := φ(x + λ_k z), so g_k ∈ F and g_k ⇀ ψ.
1. Uniqueness of weak limits in F. Let g ∈ F with ∫ f g dμ = ∫ f ψ dμ for every continuous compactly supported f; then g = ψ. Indeed, g and ψ are locally μ-integrable by (H1), and the identity holds in particular for all smooth compactly supported f. So g = ψ μ-a.e. by the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations, which holds for any Borel measure on a finite-dimensional real space and locally integrable functions (Mathlib ae_eq_of_integral_contDiff_smul_eq). Parent fact (a) gives the classical argument: on a ball B, |g − ψ|μ⌞B is a finite Borel measure; in it, the bounded sign field of each coordinate of g − ψ is an L¹-limit of continuous fields with compact support in B, which forces ∫_B |g − ψ| dμ = 0. Then g = ψ by (H0).
2. Translates of ψ lie in F. Let w ∈ ℝ^P and θ := 1/(2 + |w|). Then 0 < θ ≤ 1/2 < 1 and |θw| = θ|w| ≤ 1 − θ, since θ(1 + |w|) ≤ 1. So z ↦ ψ(θw + θz) belongs to F by (A.1). By homogeneity ψ(θw + θz) = ψ(θ(w + z)) = ψ(w + z). Hence ψ_{w,1} : z ↦ ψ(w + z) belongs to F.
3. Key step. Let w ∈ ℝ^P and c_k > 0 with c_k → 1, and suppose that for all sufficiently large k, g_k(w + z) = g_k(c_k z) for every z. Then ψ(w + z) = ψ(z) for all z. Proof: the g_k are locally integrable by (H1). Let f be continuous with compact support. The sibling lemma adr_weak_tendsto_comp_affine, with translation w and factors 1, gives ∫ f(z) g_k(w + z) dμ → ∫ f(z) ψ(w + z) dμ. With translation 0 and factors c_k, it gives ∫ f(z) g_k(c_k z) dμ → ∫ f(z) ψ(z) dμ. The two sequences of integrals agree for large k, so their limits agree: ∫ f ψ_{w,1} dμ = ∫ f ψ dμ for all such f. By steps 1 and 2, ψ_{w,1} = ψ.
4. Translations in S. Let s ∈ S. For every k and z, λ_k s ∈ S, and S-invariance of φ with λ = 1 gives g_k(s + z) = φ(λ_k s + 1·(x + λ_k z)) = φ(x + λ_k z) = g_k(1·z). Step 3 with w = s and c_k = 1 gives ψ(s + z) = ψ(z) for all z.
5. Translations along x. Let β ∈ ℝ. Since λ_k → 0, there is k₁ with a_k := 1 + βλ_k > 0 for k ≥ k₁. Put c_k := 1/a_k for k ≥ k₁ and c_k := 1 for k < k₁; then c_k > 0 and c_k → 1. For k ≥ k₁ and all z, S-invariance of φ with y = 0 ∈ S and dilation factor a_k > 0 gives g_k(βx + z) = φ(a_k x + λ_k z) = φ(a_k(x + λ_k c_k z)) = φ(x + λ_k c_k z) = g_k(c_k z). Step 3 with w = βx gives ψ(βx + z) = ψ(z) for all z.
6. Conclusion. Let y ∈ S + ℝx, say y = s + βx with s ∈ S and β ∈ ℝ, and let λ > 0 and z ∈ ℝ^P. By steps 4 and 5 and the homogeneity of ψ, ψ(y + λz) = ψ(s + (βx + λz)) = ψ(βx + λz) = ψ(λz) = ψ(z). ∎

translates ψ(w+·) of the homogeneous ψ belong to F by A.1 with θ = 1/(2+|w|)
if a translate of the blow-up sequence eventually equals a dilation of it with factors c_k → 1, then ψ is invariant under that translation (sibling adr_weak_tendsto_comp_affine twice)
S-translations commute with blow-ups, and translation by βx equals dilation by 1/(1+βλ_k) via homogeneity of φ; combine with homogeneity of ψ

The eventual positive factors 1/(1+βλ_k), together with the declared affine-convergence dependency, justify the added direction without circularity.

Source: Simon, proof of A.4, implication (1) (chapter-A.txt lines 58–112), i.e. step 5 of the parent proof. Notation is as in the statement. Let A := sing φ ∩ B_1(0). Diameters take values in [0, ∞] and 0^ℓ = 0 since ℓ > 0.
1. A is Borel (closed ∩ open, by A.3c) and bounded. By the sibling lemma adr_content_density there is a μH[ℓ]-null set N ⊆ A such that every x ∈ A ∖ N has property (D): for every δ > 0 there is ρ ∈ (0, δ) such that every countable cover {C_j} of A ∩ B_ρ(x) satisfies ρ^ℓ ≤ 2Σ_j (diam C_j)^ℓ. It suffices to show that every x ∈ A ∖ N has the required property; then the exceptional set of the statement is contained in N.
2. Fix x ∈ A ∖ N, so |x| < 1, and put δ₀ := (1 − |x|)/4. Using (D), choose ρ_0 ∈ (0, δ₀), and inductively ρ_{k+1} ∈ (0, min(ρ_k, 1/(k+1))), each satisfying the cover inequality of (D). Then ρ_k > 0, (ρ_k) is strictly decreasing, ρ_k → 0 and ρ_k < δ₀. Every countable cover {C_j} of A ∩ B_{ρ_k}(x) has ρ_k^ℓ ≤ 2Σ_j (diam C_j)^ℓ.
3. Let Λ_k := 2ρ_k. This sequence is positive, strictly decreasing, tends to 0, and Λ_k < (1 − |x|)/2. By (A.2) with y = x there are a strictly increasing sub and ψ ∈ F, homogeneous of degree zero, with φ_{x,Λ_{sub(k)}} ⇀ ψ. Put λ_k := Λ_{sub(k)}. Then λ_k > 0, λ_k < (1 − |x|)/2 ≤ 1/2 < 1, |x| ≤ 1 − λ_k, λ_k → 0, ψ ∈ F, φ_{x,λ_k} ⇀ ψ, and ψ is homogeneous. It remains to show μH[ℓ](sing ψ ∩ B_1(0)) > 0. Suppose instead that it is 0.
4. φ_k := φ_{x,λ_k} ∈ F by (A.1), and sing φ_k = {z : x + λ_k z ∈ sing φ} by (A.3(2)).
5. Small open cover. Let ε' := 2^{−ℓ}/8. The set E := sing ψ ∩ B̄_{1/2}(0) ⊆ sing ψ ∩ B_1(0) is μH[ℓ]-null. So by the definition of Hausdorff measure there are sets D_j (j ∈ ℕ) covering E with Σ_j (diam D_j)^ℓ < 2^{−ℓ−1}ε'. For nonempty D_j pick p_j ∈ D_j and r_j > diam D_j with (2r_j)^ℓ ≤ 2^ℓ(diam D_j)^ℓ + ε'2^{−j−2}, and let U_j := B_{r_j}(p_j) ⊇ D_j; let U_j := ∅ if D_j = ∅. The U_j are open, E ⊆ U := ∪_j U_j, and Σ_j (diam U_j)^ℓ ≤ Σ_j (2r_j)^ℓ < ε'. (The library lemma Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.exists_isOpen_superset_ediam_rpow_lt provides such enlargements.)

subproblem.title: Step 7: H^{d+α}(sing φ ∩ B_1(0)) = 0 for the maximal invariance dimension d
subproblem.statement: Let P, n, Q ∈ ℕ, let F be a set of functions ℝ^P → ℝ^Q, and let sing map functions to subsets of ℝ^P, with φ_{y,λ} and ⇀ as above. Assume (H0) two members of F agreeing μH[n]-a.e. are equal, (H1) members of F are locally μH[n]-integrable, and A.1, A.2, A.3c, A.3(2), A.3(3) exactly as in the parent theorem. Call ψ L-invariant (L a linear subspace) if ψ(y + λx) = ψ(x) for all y ∈ L, λ > 0 and x. Let d ∈ ℕ be such that every L-invariant ψ ∈ F with sing ψ ≠ ∅ has dim L ≤ d. Then μH[d+α](sing φ ∩ B_1(0)) = 0 for every φ ∈ F and every real α > 0.

Source: Simon, proof of A.4, chapter-A.txt lines 113–141. This is the induction on the dimension k of the invariance subspace, together with 'if ℓ > d then the above induction works up to k = d'. It is step 7 of the parent proof with departure [D3]: the new point x is taken in the full-measure set of implication (1).
1. Fix α > 0 and put ℓ := d + α > d. Every linear subspace S with dim S ≤ d is μH[ℓ]-null: S is isometric to ℝ^{dim S} and ℓ > dim S (Mathlib Real.hausdorffMeasure_of_finrank_lt applied in S, transported by the isometric inclusion S → ℝ^P).
2. Suppose some φ ∈ F has μH[ℓ](sing φ ∩ B_1(0)) > 0. We prove by induction on j = 0, 1, …, d + 1 the claim C(j): there are ψ_j ∈ F and a j-dimensional linear subspace S_j such that ψ_j is S_j-invariant and μH[ℓ](sing ψ_j ∩ B_1(0)) > 0.
3. C(0). Apply the sibling lemma adr_tangent_keeps_measure to φ and ℓ. The points of A := sing φ ∩ B_1(0) without the property stated there form a μH[ℓ]-null set. Since μH[ℓ](A) > 0, some x ∈ A has the property, which yields ψ ∈ F, homogeneous of degree zero, with μH[ℓ](sing ψ ∩ B_1(0)) > 0. Homogeneity is {0}-invariance, so C(0) holds with S_0 := {0}.
4. C(j) ⇒ C(j+1) for j ≤ d. Let A_j := sing ψ_j ∩ B_1(0). The sibling lemma adr_tangent_keeps_measure applied to ψ_j gives a μH[ℓ]-null set B_j ⊆ A_j off which its property holds. Also μH[ℓ](S_j) = 0 by step 1, since dim S_j = j ≤ d. As A_j ⊆ B_j ∪ S_j ∪ (A_j ∖ (B_j ∪ S_j)) and μH[ℓ](A_j) > 0, there is x ∈ A_j ∖ (B_j ∪ S_j). Thus x ∉ S_j, and there are λ_k with 0 < λ_k < 1, |x| ≤ 1 − λ_k and λ_k → 0, and ψ ∈ F homogeneous of degree zero, with (ψ_j)_{x,λ_k} ⇀ ψ and μH[ℓ](sing ψ ∩ B_1(0)) > 0. By (A.1), (ψ_j)_{x,λ_k} ∈ F for every k. The sibling lemma adr_tangent_invariance (with φ := ψ_j, S := S_j and this x, λ_k, ψ) shows that ψ is (S_j + ℝx)-invariant. dim(S_j + ℝx) = j + 1 because x ∉ S_j. So C(j+1) holds with ψ_{j+1} := ψ and S_{j+1} := S_j + ℝx.
5. C(d+1) gives ψ ∈ F invariant under a (d+1)-dimensional subspace with μH[ℓ](sing ψ ∩ B_1(0)) > 0, so sing ψ ≠ ∅. The hypothesis on d then gives d + 1 ≤ d, a contradiction. Hence μH[d+α](sing φ ∩ B_1(0)) = 0 for every φ ∈ F. ∎
proof_key_steps: ℓ = d+α exceeds the dimension of every subspace of dimension ≤ d, so such subspaces are μH[ℓ]-null
assuming positive μH[ℓ] measure, the sibling adr_tangent_keeps_measure yields a homogeneous member of F with positive measure (dimension 0)
at each stage choose a good point x outside the current subspace S_j (possible since μH[ℓ](S_j)=0); the sibling adr_tangent_invariance adds the direction x
after d+1 steps a member with nonempty singular set is invariant under a (d+1)-dimensional space, contradicting the bound on d

subproblem.natural_proof:
Source: Simon, proof of A.4, chapter-A.txt lines 133–139 ('sing ψ ⊇ T by A.3(2) … if there is x̃ ∈ sing ψ ∖ T … contradicting the definition of d. Therefore sing ψ = T'). This is step 8 of the parent proof.
1. For y ∈ L and λ > 0, L-invariance gives φ_{y,λ} = φ. So (A.3(2)) gives sing φ = {x : y + λx ∈ sing φ} whenever y ∈ L, 0 < λ < 1 and |y| ≤ 1 − λ, and sing φ is closed (A.3c). The sibling lemma adr_affine_invariant_closed_set with S := sing φ yields (i) y + λz ∈ sing φ ⇔ z ∈ sing φ for all y ∈ L, λ > 0 and z; and (ii) L ⊆ sing φ, since sing φ ≠ ∅.
2. Suppose some z ∈ sing φ ∖ L. Then z ≠ 0, since 0 ∈ L. Put x := z/(2|z|). By (i) with y = 0 and λ = 1/(2|z|), x ∈ sing φ. Also |x| = 1/2, and x ∉ L, since otherwise z = 2|z|x ∈ L.
3. Let Λ_k := (1/2)/(k + 2). This is a strictly decreasing positive sequence with Λ_k → 0 and Λ_k ≤ 1/4. (A.2) with y = x (|x| < 1) gives a strictly increasing sub and ψ ∈ F, homogeneous of degree zero, with φ_{x,λ_k} ⇀ ψ, where λ_k := Λ_{sub(k)}. Here 0 < λ_k ≤ 1/4 < 1, |x| = 1/2 ≤ 1 − λ_k and λ_k → 0.
4. By (A.1), φ_k := φ_{x,λ_k} ∈ F. By (A.3(2)), 0 ∈ sing φ_k because x + λ_k·0 = x ∈ sing φ, and 0 ∈ B_1(0). The sibling lemma adr_sing_mem_of_tendsto with z_k := 0 → 0 gives 0 ∈ sing ψ, so sing ψ ≠ ∅.
5. The sibling lemma adr_tangent_invariance with S := L shows that ψ is (L + ℝx)-invariant, and dim(L + ℝx) = d + 1 because x ∉ L. The hypothesis on d then gives d + 1 ≤ d, a contradiction. Hence sing φ ⊆ L, and with (ii), sing φ = L. ∎

a singular point outside L rescales to x ∈ sing φ with |x| = 1/2 and x ∉ L
A.2 at x gives a homogeneous tangent function ψ; Lemma T (sibling) gives 0 ∈ sing ψ
